text: On 11 May 1812, at approximately 5:15 pm, Spencer Perceval, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, was shot dead in the lobby of the House of Commons by John Bellingham, a Liverpool merchant who had a grievance against the government. Bellingham was detained; four days later, he was tried, convicted, and sentenced to death. He was hanged at Newgate Prison on 18 May, one week after the assassination and one month before the start of the War of 1812. Perceval remains the only British prime minister to have been assassinated. Perceval had led the Tory government since 1809 during a critical phase of the Napoleonic Wars. His strict approach to prosecuting the war led to widespread poverty and unrest on the home front, causing rejoicing in the most affected areas. Although initial fears suggested a possible general uprising, it was confirmed that Bellingham had acted alone, having been motivated by the government's failure to compensate him for his imprisonment in Russia due to a trading debt. Bellingham denied responsibility for the debt, which stemmed from losses incurred by a business associate, and believed the Russian authorities had wrongfully imprisoned him. After being released in 1809 without compensation, he repeatedly petitioned British authorities, including the Foreign Office, the Treasury, the Privy Council, and Perceval himself, all of which rejected his claims. In May 1811, after being told by his wife to abandon his campaign or lose her and his family, Bellingham moved to Liverpool. He returned to London in December 1811 to resume his efforts, again receiving polite refusals. On 20 April 1812, he purchased two .50 calibre pistols and had a tailor sew an inside pocket to his coat. On 11 May, Bellingham visited the House of Commons lobby, where he had previously made several visits, including asking journalists to verify ministerial identities. That day, he spent the morning writing letters and visiting his wife’s business partner, Mary Stevens, and in the afternoon accompanied his landlady and her son to the European Museum before arriving alone at the Palace of Westminster. As Perceval entered the lobby, Bellingham drew a pistol and shot him in the chest. Perceval staggered forward, exclaimed "I am murdered!" before falling at the feet of William Smith, the MP for Norwich, who initially mistook the body for that of William Wilberforce. Perceval was carried into the Speaker's quarters, where he was propped up on a table with a faint pulse, but died shortly after a surgeon arrived. Bellingham sat calmly during the chaos and was identified by an official and by his own MP, Isaac Gascoyne. He was taken to the Serjeant-at-Arms's quarters and later tried, convicted, and executed. Perceval's government faced significant challenges, including industrial unrest and the failure of the Walcheren Campaign, and relied heavily on the Orders in Council of 1807, which restricted trade with France and its allies, causing economic hardship in key industries such as textiles and cotton. This led to widespread petitions from regions like Yorkshire, Lancashire, Birmingham, and the Staffordshire Potteries, with over one hundred witnesses detailing the resulting poverty and distress. Critics argued that repealing the Orders was essential to restoring trade with the United States and easing domestic suffering. Perceval, a deeply religious man and a staunch evangelical, opposed Catholic emancipation and supported the abolition of the slave trade through the Slave Trade Act 1807. He was known for his opposition to radicals, imprisoning figures like Burdett and Cobbett, and introducing a bill making machine-breaking a capital offence, which Lord Byron criticized as "barbarous." Despite these difficulties, Perceval gradually gained authority, with Lord Liverpool noting in 1811 that his influence in the House equaled that of William Pitt. By May 1812, his political position was unassailable, even amid public protests. Later historians have criticized Bellingham's trial and execution as contrary to principles of justice, and a 2012 study examined the possibility that he was acting on behalf of a group of Liverpool traders opposed to Perceval's economic policies. Spencer Perceval was born on 1 November 1762, the second son of John Perceval, 2nd Earl of Egmont. He attended Harrow School and entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1780, where he was a noted scholar and prizewinner. He married Jane Wilson in 1790, and they had twelve children (six sons and six daughters) over fourteen years. After leaving Cambridge in 1783, he trained as a lawyer at Lincoln's Inn, was called to the bar in 1786, and joined the Midland Circuit, where his family connections helped secure a lucrative practice. He served as Solicitor General and then Attorney General in the Addington and Pitt ministries before becoming Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons in March 1807. When the Duke of Portland resigned in October 1809, Perceval succeeded him as First Lord of the Treasury. His government was weakened by the refusal of key ministers such as George Canning and William Huskisson, and faced opposition from the Prince of Wales, who later developed a reasonable relationship with Perceval. Perceval insisted on maintaining Wellington’s army in Portugal, a decision that was later vindicated despite significant financial cost. His opposition to the Orders in Council and his harsh policies contributed to growing public discontent, which culminated in the assassination. After Perceval's death, Parliament made generous provisions for his widow and children and approved the erection of monuments. His ministry was soon forgotten, his policies reversed, and he is generally remembered for the manner of his death rather than his achievements.

With his feet on two chairs, Perceval was senseless but still had a faint pulse; when a surgeon arrived a few minutes later, the pulse had ceased and Perceval was declared dead. In the chaos that followed, Bellingham sat quietly on a bench as Perceval was carried into the Speaker's quarters. In the lobby, the confusion was so great that, according to a witness, Bellingham "walked quietly out into the street, he would have escaped, and the committer of the murder would never have been known." Instead, an official who saw the shooting identified Bellingham, who was seized, disarmed, manhandled, and searched. He remained calm and submitted without resistance. When questioned, Bellingham stated he was rectifying a denial of justice by the government. Bellingham's own local MP, Isaac Gascoyne, who was present at the shooting, also identified him. The Speaker ordered Bellingham transferred to the Serjeant-at-Arms's quarters, where MPs who were magistrates conducted a committal hearing chaired by Harvey Christian Combe. The makeshift court heard eyewitness accounts and sent messengers to search Bellingham's lodgings. Bellingham kept his composure; although warned against self-incrimination, he insisted on explaining himself, saying, "I have been ill-treated... I have sought redress in vain. I am a most unfortunate man and feel here"—placing hand on heart—"sufficient justification for what I have done." He claimed he had exhausted all proper avenues and had made it clear to authorities he would take independent action, and had been told to do his worst: "I have obeyed them. I have done my worst, and I rejoice in the deed." Around eight o'clock, Bellingham was formally charged with Perceval's murder and committed to Newgate Prison to await trial. Reports of the assassination spread quickly; Arthur Bryant recorded that hungry workers, who had suffered under Perceval's government, received the news with crude delight. William Cobbett, then imprisoned for seditious libel, wrote that the shooting had "ridded them of one whom they looked upon as the leader among those whom they thought totally bent on the destruction of their liberties." The scenes outside the Palace of Westminster as Bellingham was taken to Newgate reflected this mood; Samuel Romilly, MP for Wareham, heard from the crowd "the most savage expressions of joy and exultation... accompanied with regret that others, and particularly the attorney general, had not shared the same fate." The crowd surged around the hackney coach carrying Bellingham; many tried to shake his hand, others mounted the coach-box and had to be beaten off with whips. Bellingham was hustled back into the building and kept there until the disorder subsided enough for him to be moved with a full military escort. Among the governing classes, there were initial fears the assassination might be part of a general insurrection or spark one. The authorities responded by deploying the Foot Guards and mounted troops, the City militia, and reinforcing local watches. In contrast, Perceval's friends and colleagues expressed sombre sorrow. When Parliament met the next day, Canning said of Perceval, "a man... of whom it might with particular truth be said that, whatever was the strength of political hostility, he had never before that last calamity provoked a single enemy." After further tributes from both government and opposition members, the House passed a grant of £50,000 and an annuity of £2,000 to Perceval's widow, a provision slightly amended and approved in June. Perceval's high regard among peers was evident in an anonymous 1812 poem, "Universal Sympathy, or, The Martyr'd Statesman," which stated: "Such was his private, such his public life, That all who differed in polemic strife, Or varied in opinion with his plan, Agreed with one accord to love the man." An inquest into Perceval's death was held on 12 May at the Rose and Crown public house in Downing Street. Among those who testified were Gascoyne, Smith, and Joseph Hume, a doctor and Radical MP. Hume, who had helped detain Bellingham, testified that Bellingham appeared "perfectly sane" after the shooting. The coroner registered the cause of death as "wilful murder by John Bellingham." Armed with this verdict, the Attorney General, Sir Vicary Gibbs, requested the Lord Chief Justice to arrange the earliest possible trial date. In Newgate Prison, Bellingham was questioned by magistrates. His calm demeanour and poise led them, unlike Hume, to doubt his sanity, although his keepers observed no signs of unbalanced behaviour. James Harmer, Bellingham's solicitor, knew that insanity would be the only conceivable defence and dispatched agents to Liverpool to investigate. While awaiting reports, he learned from an informant that Bellingham's father had died insane; he also heard from Ann Billett, the prisoner's cousin, who had known him from childhood, about his supposed derangement. On 14 May, a grand jury met in the Sessions House, Clerkenwell, and after hearing eyewitness evidence, found "a true Bill against John Bellingham for the murder of Spencer Perceval." The trial was scheduled for the next day, Friday 15 May 1812, at the Old Bailey. When Bellingham learned of his trial, he asked Harmer to arrange for him to be represented by Brougham and Peter Alley, the latter known for flamboyance. Confident of acquittal, Bellingham refused further discussion with Harmer and spent the afternoon and evening making notes. After drinking a glass of porter, he went to bed and slept soundly. Bellingham's trial began at the Old Bailey on Friday 15 May 1812, presided over by Sir James Mansfield, Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas. The prosecution was led by Attorney General Gibbs, assisted by William Garrow, a future Attorney General. Brougham declined, so Bellingham was represented by Alley, assisted by Henry Revell Reynolds. At the time, defending counsel in capital cases had limited roles: they could advise on points of law, examine and cross-examine witnesses, but otherwise Bellingham had to present his own defence. After entering a not guilty plea, Alley requested a postponement to allow time to locate witnesses to Bellingham's insanity. Gibbs opposed this as a mere delay of justice; Mansfield agreed, and the trial proceeded. Gibbs described Bellingham's business activities before misfortune in Russia—"whether through his own misconduct or by the justice or injustice of that country, I know not"—and recounted his unsuccessful attempts to obtain redress and the resulting desire for revenge. Having described the shooting, Gibbs dismissed the possibility of insanity, asserting Bellingham was fully in control at the time of the deed. Numerous eyewitnesses testified to what they saw in the Commons lobby. The court also heard from a tailor who, before the attack, had, at Bellingham's instruction, modified his coat by adding a special inside pocket, in which Bellingham had concealed his pistols. When Bellingham rose, he thanked Gibbs for rejecting the "insanity" strategy: "I think it is far more fortunate that such a plea... should have been unfounded, than it should have existed in fact." He began his defence by asserting that "all the miseries which it is possible for human nature to endure" had fallen on him. He then read the petition he had sent to the Prince Regent and recalled his fruitless dealings with government agencies. In his view, the main blame lay not with "that truly amiable and highly lamented individual, Mr Perceval," but with Leveson-Gower, the ambassador in St Petersburg, who he believed had originally denied him justice and deserved the shot rather than Perceval. Bellingham's main witnesses were Ann Billett and her friend Mary Clarke, both of whom testified to his history of derangement, and Catherine Figgins, a servant in Bellingham's lodgings, who said she found him recently confused but otherwise honest and admirable. As she stood down, Alley informed the court that two more witnesses had arrived from Liverpool. However, when they saw Bellingham, they realized he was not the man whose derangement they had come to attest and withdrew. Mansfield then began his summing up, clarifying the law: "The single question is whether at the time this act was committed, he possessed a sufficient degree of understanding to distinguish good from evil, right from wrong." He advised the jury that the evidence showed Bellingham to be "in every respect a full and competent judge of all his actions." The jury retired and returned with a guilty verdict within fifteen minutes. Bellingham appeared surprised but, according to Thomas Hodgson's account, remained calm, "without any demonstrations of that concern which the awfulness of his situation was calculate to produce." When asked by the court clerk if he had anything to say, he remained silent. The judge then read the sentence, Hodgson records, "in a most solemn and affecting manner, which bathed many of the auditors in tears." He condemned the crime as "odious and abominable in the eyes of God as it is hateful and abhorrent to the feelings of man." He reminded the prisoner of the short time—"a very short time"—he had left to seek mercy in another world, and then pronounced the sentence of death: "You shall be hanged by the neck until you be dead, your body to be dissected and anatomized." The entire trial lasted less than eight hours. Bellingham's execution was fixed for the morning of Monday 18 May. The day before, he was visited by the Revd Daniel Wilson, curate at St John's Chapel, Bedford Row, a future Bishop of Calcutta, who hoped Bellingham would show true repentance. Wilson was disappointed, concluding that "a more dreadful instance of depravity and hardness of heart has surely never occurred." Late on Sunday, Bellingham wrote a last letter to his wife, in which he appeared confident of his soul's destination: "Nine hours more will waft me to those happy shores where bliss is without alloy." Large crowds gathered outside Newgate Prison on 18 May; a force of troops stood by due to warnings of a "Rescue Bellingham" movement. The crowd was calm and restrained, and Bellingham, when he appeared at the scaffold shortly before 8 o'clock, moved "with the utmost celerity... his tread was bold and firm... no indication of trembling, faltering, or irresolution appeared." He was then blindfolded, the rope fastened, and a final prayer was said by the chaplain. As the clock struck eight, the trap door was released, and Bellingham dropped to his death. Cobbett, still incarcerated in Newgate, observed the crowd's reactions: "anxious looks... half-horrified countenances... mournful tears... unanimous blessings." In accordance with the sentence, the body was cut down and sent to St Bartholomew's Hospital for dissection. In what the press described as "morbid sensationalism," Bellingham's clothes were sold for high prices to members of the public. On 15 May, the House of Commons voted to erect a monument to Perceval in Westminster Abbey. Later, memorials were placed in Lincoln's Inn and within Perceval's Northampton constituency. There is also a memorial to Perceval in St Luke's Church, Charlton, where he was buried, in the form of a bust and his brother's hatchment with the Perceval coat of arms. On 8 June, the Regent appointed Lord Liverpool to head a new Tory administration. Despite eulogies to their fallen leader, members of the new government soon began to distance themselves from his ministry. Many of the changes Perceval had opposed were gradually introduced: greater press freedom, Catholic emancipation, and parliamentary reform. The 1807 Orders in Council were repealed on 23 June, but too late to avoid the United States declaring war on the United Kingdom. Lord Liverpool's government did not maintain Perceval's resolution in acting against the illegal slave trade, which began to flourish as authorities looked the other way. British historian Andro Linklater estimates that around 40,000 slaves were illegally transported from Africa to the West Indies due to lax enforcement. Linklater cites Perceval's greatest achievement as his insistence on keeping Wellington's army in the field, a policy that helped turn the tide in the Napoleonic Wars decisively in Britain's favour. Despite this, Perceval's reputation faded over time; Charles Dickens considered him "a third-rate politician scarcely fit to carry Lord Chatham's crutch." In due course, little but the fact of his assassination remained in public memory. As the bicentenary of the shooting approached, Perceval was described in newspapers as "the prime minister that history forgot." The justice of Bellingham's conviction was first questioned by Brougham, who condemned the trial as "the greatest disgrace to English justice." In a 2004 study, American academic Kathleen S. Goddard criticises the timing of the trial so soon after the act, when passions were high, and points out the court's refusal to allow an adjournment to permit the defence to contact witnesses. She maintains there was insufficient evidence to determine Bellingham's sanity and that Mansfield's summing-up showed significant bias. Bellingham's claim to have acted alone was accepted in court; Linklater's 2012 study suggests he could have been an agent of other interests—perhaps Liverpool merchants, who bore the main brunt of Perceval's economic policies and had much to gain by his demise. Comments by a Liverpool newspaper, says Linklater, indicate that talk of assassination was common in the city. It remains unknown how Bellingham gained funds to spend freely in the months before the assassination, when he was not engaged in any business. This conspiracy theory has not convinced other historians; columnist Bruce Anderson points to the lack of concrete evidence. In the months after her husband's execution, Mary Bellingham continued to live and work in Liverpool. By the end of 1812 her business had failed, and thereafter her movements are obscure; she may have reverted to her maiden name. In January 1815, Jane Perceval married Sir Henry William Carr; she died, aged 74, in 1844. In 1828, The Times reported that Cornish industrialist landowner John Williams the Third (1753–1841) received a dream warning of Perceval's assassination on 2 or 3 May 1812, nearly ten days before the event, "correct in every detail." Perceval himself had a series of dreams culminating on 10 May with one of his own death, which he had while spending the night at the house of the Earl of Harrowby. He told the Earl of his dream, and the Earl tried to persuade Perceval not to attend Parliament that day, but Perceval refused to be scared off by "a mere dream" and headed for Westminster on the afternoon of 11 May. A distant kinsman of the assassin, Henry Bellingham, became Conservative MP for North West Norfolk in 1983 and held junior office in the Cameron–Clegg coalition of 2010–2015. When he temporarily lost his seat in 1997—he regained it in 2001—his narrow defeat was widely regarded as arising from the intervention of Roger Percival, the candidate for the Referendum Party whose votes largely came from disgruntled Conservatives. Despite the different spelling, media accounts asserted Percival's descent from the assassinated prime minister's family and reported the defeat as a belated form of revenge. Ham became a Conservative MP for North West Norfolk in 1983 and held junior office in the Cameron–Clegg coalition from 2010 to 2015. When he temporarily lost his seat in 1997—regaining it in 2001—his narrow defeat was widely attributed to Roger Percival, the Referendum Party candidate whose votes primarily came from disgruntled Conservatives. Despite the different spelling, media accounts claimed Percival descended from the family of the assassinated prime minister and reported the defeat as a form of belated revenge. The majority of the Palace of Westminster (excluding Westminster Hall) that existed at the time of the assassination was destroyed by an accidental fire in 1834, after which the Houses were comprehensively rebuilt and expanded. In July 2014, a brass memorial plaque was unveiled in St Stephen's Hall, Houses of Parliament, near where Perceval was killed. Michael Ellis, Conservative MP for Northampton North (part of Perceval's former Northampton constituency), had campaigned for the plaque following the removal of four patterned floor tiles that were said to mark the spot during a recent renovation.
